detail.abstract: Mid-sized businesses are vital to the U.S. economy, contributing more than 30% of national GDP and supporting millions of jobs. However, most corporate governance frameworks, such as those established under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX) and the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, are designed for large public companies, leaving mid-sized enterprises without tailored guidance. This governance gap often leads to concentrated decision-making, inadequate oversight, succession risks, and limited investor confidence. The purpose of this article is to propose adaptable, affordable, and legally grounded governance models suited to the mid-market. Drawing on the Delaware General Corporation Law, the Model Business Corporation Act (MBCA), and fiduciary duty standards from In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, the article introduces practical mechanisms including scalable board structures, lightweight audit and risk committees, governance charters, digital tools, and voluntary ESG alignment. A phased implementation roadmap is also provided to ensure firms can adopt these practices gradually and cost-effectively. By presenting a pragmatic blueprint, the article demonstrates that right-sized governance is a compliance tool and a strategic enabler of resilience, investor trust, and sustainable growth in mid-sized American businesses.

title: Artificial Vertical Market Integration in U.S. Healthcare: A Competition Economics Framework for Analyzing Insurer-Provider PBM Consolidation

detail.title: Artificial Vertical Market Integration in U.S. Healthcare: A Competition Economics Framework for Analyzing Insurer-Provider PBM Consolidation
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Artificial Vertical Market Integration (AVMI)-a novel analytical framework for understanding competitive harms arising from consolidation patterns in U.S. healthcare markets that evade traditional antitrust scrutiny. Unlike organic vertical integration driven by transaction cost efficiencies, AVMI describes strategic acquisitions designed to create rent extraction points across the healthcare value chain while maintaining the appearance of independent market participants. Using UnitedHealth Group's integration of UnitedHealthcare (insurance), Optum (provider services and 90,000+ physicians), and OptumRx (pharmacy benefit management) as the paradigmatic case study, this paper demonstrates how vertically integrated healthcare conglomerates can leverage multi-market presence to foreclose competition, inflate costs, and steer patients toward affiliated entities-all while passing cursory horizontal merger review. The paper proposes a revised antitrust framework specifically calibrated to healthcare markets, incorporating 'extraction point analysis' as a complement to traditional market concentration metrics. Policy recommendations include presumptive illegality for certain cross-segment acquisitions, mandatory divestiture triggers based on market share across integrated segments, and enhanced FTC/DOJ coordination for pattern-of-acquisition analysis. This framework addresses a critical gap in competition economics literature, which has historically treated vertical integration in healthcare as efficiency-enhancing rather than potentially foreclosure-creating.

detail.abstract: This project studies international uncertainty links between Australia and other countries using a Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) algorithm. I use indexes of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) first developed by Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2015) to examine how EPU in Australia is linked to EPU in other countries. This project replicates research by Gupta, Pierdzioch, and Risse (2016), who studied how EPU in Canada is linked to EPU in seven other countries using a BART algorithm. I find Australian EPU is more strongly linked to the Indo-Pacific region than Anglosphere countries.

title: LLM-Driven Drift Models for Brownian Motion in Quantitative Finance
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: LLM-Driven Drift Models for Brownian Motion in Quantitative Finance
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) capture rich semantic information from unstructured financial text, while Brownian motion and stochastic differential equations (SDEs) remain the canonical tools for modeling continuous-time asset dynamics. However, existing approaches typically keep these two worlds separate: continuous-time models rely on parametric drifts and volatilities, whereas LLMs are used only in discrete-time prediction or qualitative analysis. This paper proposes a rigorous framework for LLM-driven drift SDEs, in which the drift of a Brownian-motion model is a measurable, learned functional of an LLM-derived representation of the market context. We formalize the model, establish existence and uniqueness of strong solutions under natural regularity conditions, and study the induced risk-neutral measures. On the statistical side, we analyze a drift estimation procedure based on empirical risk minimization with LLM features and give sufficient conditions for consistency. Empirically, we instantiate the framework on equity and index futures, using a pretrained LLM to encode news and order-book commentary into low-dimensional embeddings. We then extend the basic model to an LLM-conditioned volatility specification in which the diffusion coefficient depends on the same embeddings. Across a battery of experimentsincluding return forecasting, hitting-time calibration, and quadratic-variation decomposition by LLM-identified regimes-LLM-driven SDEs match or outperform classical parametric models and black-box deep time-series baselines, while retaining a clean stochastic-process interpretation.

This OutRush report explores the characteristics, experiences, and motivations of Russian emigrants in Latin America, focusing primarily on those who left after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Based on responses from 938 participants, the report highlights that post-war emigrants primarily moved due to political reasons, safety concerns, and the threat of mobilization. Most emigrants chose Latin American countries due to political freedom, ease of residency, and naturalization opportunities.

Key findings include the balanced gender distribution among migrants, their high education levels, and significant entrepreneurial engagement. Although generally optimistic, emigrants face challenges such as bureaucratic barriers, economic instability, language difficulties, and security concerns. The report also notes strong social integration efforts, low discrimination levels, and ongoing interest in Russian politics, underscoring the emigrants' dual identities and aspirations for a politically improved homeland.

detail.abstract: Smart textiles, or electronic textiles (e-textiles), are fabrics engineered to sense, actuate, communicate, and harvest energy while retaining the flexibility and mechanical properties of conventional textiles. Although applications in health, sport, and human-computer interaction are relatively mature, their integration into transportation systems and infrastructure remains fragmented. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) that synthesizes research on smart textiles across both mobility assets and civil infrastructure. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, records were retrieved from Scopus and complementary databases, screened with defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and appraised for methodological quality. A total of 73 studies were analyzed across four clusters: (i) vehicle human-machine interface (HMI), (ii) vulnerable road user (VRU) wearables, (iii) freight and transit systems, and (iv) pavements and geostructures. Results show that capacitive and resistive e-textiles in seats and belts enhance occupant detection and posture monitoring but lack long-term validation; VRU wearables improve conspicuity and crash detection yet face challenges of washability and power autonomy; textile-based RFID and chipless sensors support inventory control and transit occupancy sensing but require standardization for real-world use; and fiber Bragg grating (FBG) and distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) embedded in pavements, slopes, and retaining walls are the most field-ready technologies, providing structural health monitoring and seepage detection. The review identifies gaps in standardization, cooperative sensing, and lifecycle durability while recommending hybrid textile-infrastructure architectures and co-designed multifunctional fabrics. This synthesis is the first to bridge vehicle, user, freight, and infrastructure applications, highlighting cross-domain pathways for advancing safe, sustainable, and intelligent transportation networks.

title: The Definition of Kokoro, A Non-Ideological Systems Theory, Something Beyond Trust, and Incidentally, a Theory of Japanese Culture
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Definition of Kokoro, A Non-Ideological Systems Theory, Something Beyond Trust, and Incidentally, a Theory of Japanese Culture
detail.abstract:
Abstract: The Definition of Kokoro, Trust as Systems Theory, and "Something Beyond Trust"

Our society runs on trust. However, much of this is an "insurance-like" trust, designed on the premise of betrayal. Economies and institutions are fundamentally based on "estimating the worst case and mitigating damage." In zero-sum games, this is the minimax principle; in general-sum games, it is the Nash Equilibrium.

Yet, there is a higher level. When a relationship exists where we are confident not only that the other will not betray us, but that they will choose the good beyond their own self-interest, we can shift our helm from risk minimization to value maximization. This is where Confucian Chūjo (devoted sincerity and the wisdom to gauge others by oneself), the Buddhist Four Immeasurables (Jihikisha: loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity), and Christian Agapē come into play. The common core is ungrudging generosity.

To rephrase this in systems theory:

  1. Virtue (Kokoro): The attitude of making others' concerns one's own.

  2. Action: Giving / Sympathetic joy / Letting go of attachment.

  3. Institution: Amplifying and insuring the effects of virtue through transparency, consistency, and accountability.

Trust cannot stand on (3) alone. (1) is the leading indicator, (2) is the daily operation, and (3) prepares for external shocks.

There are real-world examples in economics. The Omi merchants' Sanpō Yoshi ("three-way good": for seller, buyer, and society) is a classic case of kokoro-based trust lowering transaction costs and creating positive externalities. As a community matures, in some rare cases, a "Nihō Yoshi" ("two-way good": for others and society) implicitly operates. Here, even without explicitly stating "good for self," giving (gifting) circulates, and the fear of scarcity diminishes. At this stage, trust is no longer a conscious object but a saturated environment. Institutional costs lighten, and resources available for creation increase.

So, what is Kokoro? The character originates from a pictograph of the heart, and many virtues feature the 'heart' radical (心/忄). In Japanese thought, it was passed down from the ancient Seimeishin (pure/bright heart), to the medieval Shōjiki (honesty), to the early-modern Makoto (sincerity). I wish to define Kokoro as the internal engine that attenuates fear and drives giving (gifting).

Conclusion: Trust is not a substitute for monitoring; it is a device for amplifying the act of giving. From a design optimized for fear, to a design premised on ungrudging generosity. When we reassemble in the order of Kokoro (Virtue) -> Action -> Institution, we can transition from a "world of risk minimization" to a "world of value maximization."

title: The Perilous Path of Paradigm Challenge: A Case Study on the Reception of Wave Mechanics Theory in Microwave Absorption Research
affiliations: Shenyang Normal University

detail.title: The Perilous Path of Paradigm Challenge: A Case Study on the Reception of Wave Mechanics Theory in Microwave Absorption Research
detail.abstract: This article presents a critical self-reflection on the publication journey and subsequent academic reception of our work on the wave mechanics theory of microwave absorption. We detail a consistent pattern of severe difficulty in publishing, where manuscripts were accepted only by journals after numerous rejections elsewhere. We observe a conspicuous absence of formal scholarly rebuttals from editors or reviewers who previously rejected our work, or from authors whose publications on the opposing impedance matching theory we have publicly criticized. Instead, the observed responses include the continued publication of impedancematching-based work without engaging with our critique, strategic citation practices that ignore our work, and the active suppression of our critical perspectives by journals, preprint servers, and online platforms. We argue that this ecosystem-characterized by rejection without substantive critique, avoidance of direct scholarly debate, and suppression rather than refutation-represents a significant dysfunction within the modern scientific environment. It stifles legitimate paradigm challenges and hinders scientific progress.

title: The Paradox of Collective Genius: Reconciling Individual Achievement with Collaborative Innovation

detail.title: The Paradox of Collective Genius: Reconciling Individual Achievement with Collaborative Innovation
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly recognize that complex challenges demand collaborative solutions, yet Western management practices continue privileging individual achievement over collective capability. This paradox-celebrating collaboration rhetorically while structurally rewarding individual geniusundermines innovation potential and organizational resilience. Drawing on research in organizational behavior, innovation studies, and cross-cultural management, this article examines why collective genius remains elusive despite widespread acknowledgment of its importance. We analyze the organizational and individual consequences of this misalignment, review evidence-based interventions that foster genuine collaboration, and propose frameworks for building sustained collective capability. The analysis integrates empirical research with organizational examples across healthcare, technology, and creative industries, demonstrating that collective genius requires deliberate structural design rather than aspirational rhetoric. For practitioners, the core insight is clear: unlocking collective genius demands fundamental shifts in reward systems, decision-making processes, and leadership mindsets that privilege co-creation over individual heroism.

detail.abstract: This Article explores how American law created and operationalized the category of “white” from the nation’s founding through the early twentieth century, not within any single doctrinal silo, but across the full architecture of membership, capacity, and civic authority. It argues that whiteness emerged not as a natural or intuitive classification but as a legally manufactured identity policed by the judiciary in naturalization law, constitutional law, state criminal adjudication, professional licensure, and property and alienage regulation. Beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 and the racial lexicon supplied by legal dictionaries, encyclopedias, and census manuals, courts translated contested cultural understandings of race into juridical facts. Federal judges constructed a racial taxonomy in the prerequisite cases from Ah Yup to Thind; the Supreme Court constitutionalized racial identity as a boundary of sovereignty in Fong Yue Ting and as a conditional form of membership in Wong Kim Ark. State courts then absorbed and repurposed these federal definitions in miscegenation prosecutions, evidentiary competency rules, and school segregation cases from Rice v. Gong Lum to Bond v. Tij Fung, relying on visual inspection, community reputation, and folk racial grammars to assign legal identity in the courtroom. At the same time, licensing boards, bar admission rules, hospital charters, and alien land laws converted whiteness into a credential of civic trust and economic authority, excluding Asian immigrants and nonwhite professionals from the professions, skilled trades, and landholding through the category of the “alien ineligible for citizenship.” Across these domains, law acted as both mirror and mold: mirroring prevailing racial hierarchies even as it molded whiteness into a legal personhood, a status that structured who could belong, who could speak with professional authority, who could hold land, and who the state treated as perpetually foreign. This Article concludes by showing how this architecture of legal whiteness continues to shape contemporary debates over citizenship verification, professional licensing, and the racialization of foreignness long after the formal dismantling of racial prerequisites.

title: Connecting the Dots in Lean Implementation -Insights from Qualitative Data Analysis in Croatian Lean Companies

detail.title: Connecting the Dots in Lean Implementation -Insights from Qualitative Data Analysis in Croatian Lean Companies
detail.abstract: Lean approach originated with the Toyota principles and philosophy of production, expended to lean methodology, lean thinking and lean culture just to name a few. The underlying principles of lean, focusing on cost reduction and waste elimination, increasing efficiency and effectiveness of business processes, gained a revival role in Industry 4.0 and started to focus even more on the agile and innovation approach with the mission of business processes continuous improvement. Although present in the literature for the past five decades, lean implementation faces lower levels of success. The reasons could be grouped by identifying challenges, obstacles and key success factors applying a contingent approach to business depending on the industry, country, level of knowledge and readiness for lean implementation. This paper uses qualitative methods, more specifically the thematic method of analysis in order not just to identify the existing dots-key factors in the literature on lean implementation but to offer a way how to connect them. The proposed model is based on the qualitative analysis of 17 lean managers from 11 Croatian lean companies. The model incorporates two hierarchy levels, four iteration processes and five steps in lean implementation. The paper is in line with the findings of the literature on change management adjusted to the case of lean implementation. The model could be used for educational purposes in lean training and business improvement interventions. The next research step is to further build validation of the model by testing it within and across different cultures and industries.
